before.content_html:
Rome and the Greek Gods

When the Romans encountered the Greek world from around the third century BC onwards, they found a pantheon of deities that mapped closely — though not perfectly — onto their own. The Romans absorbed and adapted Greek mythology with extraordinary thoroughness, giving Greek gods Roman names and integrating their stories into Roman religion and literature. Understanding where the correspondence is close, where it differs, and what those differences reveal about each culture is one of the most important analytical skills in this subject.

The key Roman Olympians were: Jupiter, Juno, Neptune, Vulcan, Mercury, Mars, Pluto, Apollo, Juno, Venus, Minerva, Diana, Bacchus, Vesta and Ceres. Apollo was adopted directly into Roman religion without a name change — one of very few deities to retain his Greek name.

Key Fact

The principal Greek–Roman equivalences: Zeus → Jupiter; Hera → Juno; Poseidon → Neptune; Hephaistos → Vulcan; Ares → Mars; Hermes → Mercury; Artemis → Diana; Aphrodite → Venus; Demeter → Ceres; Dionysos → Bacchus; Athena → Minerva; Hestia → Vesta; Hades → Pluto. Apollo kept his Greek name in Roman religion.

How Roman Religion Adapted Greek Myth

Roman religion was originally quite different from the Greek tradition. Early Roman religion was highly ritual-focused: the Romans believed that correct performance of religious acts (the right words, the right gestures, the right offerings at the right time) maintained the pax deorum — the “peace of the gods” — which guaranteed Rome’s prosperity and safety. The gods were powerful forces to be kept on side through meticulous ritual, and initially the Romans were less interested in myths about the gods’ personal lives than the Greeks were.

As Rome came into sustained contact with the Greek world — through trade, conquest and the presence of Greek communities in southern Italy — Roman writers began actively adopting Greek myths. The poets Virgil and Ovid in particular wove Greek mythology into their Latin masterworks. Virgil’s Aeneid traces Rome’s origins to the Trojan hero Aeneas, inserting Rome into the whole framework of Greek myth. Ovid’s Metamorphoses retold hundreds of Greek mythological stories for a Roman audience, giving the Roman gods Greek names in many episodes.

Mars illustrates how a Roman deity could share a Greek counterpart but occupy a completely different cultural position. The Greek god Ares was widely disliked in Greek mythology — portrayed as brutal, bloodthirsty and often cowardly, mocked even by his fellow Olympians. Mars, by contrast, was second only to Jupiter in Roman religious importance. He was the divine father of Romulus, the founder of Rome, and the protector of Roman armies. His importance to the Roman state was vastly greater than Ares’s importance to any Greek city-state. This difference reflects the Romans’ emphasis on military power and expansion as core national values.

Jupiter, Juno and the Capitoline Triad

Jupiter was Rome’s supreme deity, the equivalent of Zeus as king of the gods and ruler of sky and thunder. Yet Jupiter had a more formal, political dimension in Roman religion than Zeus possessed in Greece. The great Capitoline Temple in Rome was dedicated not just to Jupiter but to the Capitoline Triad: Jupiter, Juno and Minerva, worshipped together as the protective trinity of the Roman state. This formal grouping of three gods as an official state cult has no direct Greek equivalent and represents a distinctly Roman religious development. Juno (equivalent to Greek Hera) was queen of the gods and particularly associated with women, marriage and childbirth, as well as the protection of the Roman state. Unlike the often vindictive and jealous Hera of Greek myth, Juno’s official Roman persona was more dignified and her role in state religion was considerably more prominent.

Key Fact

In Roman religion, the gods served a strongly civic and military function. Jupiter guaranteed Rome’s supremacy; Mars protected her armies; Vesta (goddess of the hearth) maintained the eternal flame symbolic of Rome’s continuity. The Capitoline Triad — Jupiter, Juno, Minerva — was the heart of official Roman state religion, worshipped on the Capitoline Hill.

Differences in How Gods Were Represented in Roman Art

Roman artists inherited the Greek tradition of anthropomorphic representation and continued to show gods in human form. However, the emphasis in Roman art shifted. Where Greek art often showed gods in active, mythological moments (Zeus hurling the thunderbolt; Athena emerging from his head), Roman art frequently used gods to make political statements. The Augustus of Prima Porta — a marble statue now in the Vatican Museum — is the most spectacular example. Augustus stands in a military pose, his arm raised in an oratorical gesture, wearing armour whose breastplate carries a cosmic scene: the sky god (Caelus) above, the earth goddess (Terra) below, and a Roman general receiving back the standards captured by the Parthians. At the base of the statue is Cupid riding a dolphin, a reference to Augustus’s claimed divine descent through Venus via his adoptive father Julius Caesar. The statue thus weaves together military victory, cosmic order, divine ancestry and political authority in a single image.

The Ara Pacis (Altar of Augustan Peace) offers a complementary example. Completed in 9 BC, it was a marble altar enclosed by carved walls depicting both a solemn procession of the imperial family and mythological relief panels. One panel shows the goddess Roma seated as a warrior; another shows Aeneas making sacrifice at the altar, linking Augustus directly to the Trojan hero and thus to Venus and the gods. The mythological scenes are not entertainment — they are political theology, embedding Augustus’s rule within a divine narrative of Rome’s destined greatness.

Greek religion placed great emphasis on myth — the stories of the gods’ personalities, quarrels, loves and adventures were central to how ordinary people understood the divine world. The gods in Greek religion were vividly individual and often humanly flawed. Roman religion, particularly in its official state form, was more procedural: the correct performance of ritual (and the maintenance of the pax deorum) was more important than narrative or personal devotion to a specific god’s character. A Roman farmer would pray to the appropriate deity for a good harvest not because he believed that deity had an interesting personal history, but because performing the right rite would secure divine favour. This difference does not mean Romans were less religious — they were deeply so — but the centre of gravity was different: Greek religion was mythological; Roman religion was ritual.

Why Cities Needed Foundation Myths

Every great city of the ancient world told stories about how it came to exist. These were not simply fairy tales: foundation myths gave a city its identity, its prestige and its claim to divine protection. They answered the question “why are we here, and why does this city deserve to flourish?” by anchoring the answer in the actions of gods and heroes. Athens claimed the goddess Athena as its patron; Rome traced its ancestry to the Trojan hero Aeneas and through him to the goddess Venus. These stories were told and retold in art, literature and public ritual — they shaped how citizens understood their city and its place in the world.

The Naming of Athens: Athena and Poseidon

The Athenians told a story of a divine contest for their city. Two Olympians — Athena and Poseidon — both wanted to be patron of the new city, and Zeus ruled that the one who gave the most useful gift to the citizens would win. Poseidon struck the ground of the Acropolis with his trident and a spring of salt water gushed forth — powerful, dramatic, a reminder of his dominion over the sea. Athena struck the earth and an olive tree grew. The citizens (in some versions, judged by the gods; in others, by the people themselves, with the women voting for Athena) chose the olive tree, and Athena became the city’s patron. The city was named Athens in her honour.

The olive tree was enormously meaningful to Greek life: olive oil was food, fuel for lamps, and a sacred substance used in religious ritual and to anoint the bodies of athletes. Athena’s gift was practical where Poseidon’s was merely impressive. The myth encoded a civic value: wisdom and usefulness matter more than raw power. The sacred olive tree on the Acropolis was tended as a holy relic for centuries. Ancient sources reported that when the Persians burned Athens in 480 BC, the tree sprouted new shoots the very next day — a sign, the Athenians said, of Athena’s undying protection.

Key Fact

The contest between Athena and Poseidon was depicted on the west pediment of the Parthenon, the most prominent sculptural programme in Athens. Both deities were shown at the moment of the contest, flanked by the Olympian gods as witnesses. By placing this myth at the heart of their most sacred building, the Athenians permanently embedded their divine foundation story in stone.

Theseus and the Adventures of Athens’s Hero-King

Athens also celebrated Theseus, its own heroic founder-king, whose adventures were displayed on the Theseus Kylix, now in the British Museum (catalogue number 1850,0302.3). This red-figure cup, made around 440 BC, shows seven episodes in total: the Minotaur at the centre (tondo), and six bandit and monster encounters on the outer ring — Kerkyon, Prokrustes, Skiron, the Bull of Marathon, Sinis and the Krommyonian Sow. The cup is a striking example of how a single portable object could carry an entire heroic biography. The choice of adventures depicted sends a political message: Theseus makes the roads and the sea safe, he defeats the monstrous enemy, he brings civilisation — just as Athens itself claimed to do for the Greek world.

The Founding of Rome: Romulus and Remus

Rome’s foundation myth was recorded by the historian Livy in his Early History of Rome (Book 1). According to Livy, the twins Romulus and Remus were descended from the Trojan hero Aeneas through the line of kings of Alba Longa. Their mother was a Vestal Virgin, Rhea Silvia, who had been made a priestess to prevent her from having children (and thus potential heirs who might threaten the king). The god Mars, however, came to her and fathered the twins — giving Rome its legendary divine ancestry through the god of war.

The king ordered the infants to be drowned in the Tiber, but the river was in flood and the basket carrying them was set down on dry land instead, at the foot of the Palatine Hill. There, according to Livy, a she-wolf found the abandoned infants and suckled them; later they were found and raised by a shepherd and his wife. When they grew up, they overthrew the wicked king and decided to found their own city. A dispute arose over which of two hills to build it on, and an argument about the omens (Romulus saw twelve vultures; Remus saw six) led to Romulus killing Remus. Romulus then built Rome and became its first king.

Key Fact

Livy presents the Romulus and Remus myth as reflecting key Roman values: the twins were suckled by a she-wolf (strength and ferocity), raised by a shepherd (humble origins, closeness to the land), and their divine father was Mars (Rome’s military destiny). The killing of Remus was a disturbing detail, but it established that Rome would have one founder, one king, one destiny — not a divided city.

Aeneas and the Trojan Origins of Rome

Before Romulus and Remus, Rome traced its ultimate origins even further back, to Aeneas, a Trojan prince and son of the goddess Venus. Livy records that after the fall of Troy, Aeneas led a band of survivors westward, eventually arriving in Italy and founding a settlement at Alba Longa, whose line of kings eventually included Rhea Silvia — and thus Romulus and Remus. This Trojan origin story served a brilliant political function: it made Rome part of the Greek mythological world (Troy was a major player in the greatest of all Greek myths, the Trojan War) while simultaneously asserting Roman independence — they were not Greek, they were Trojans, the Greeks’ defeated enemies, reborn as something far greater. Virgil’s Aeneid made this origin story the national epic of Rome.

Plutarch, writing in the late first century AD, wrote biographies of famous Greeks and Romans in parallel pairs, each pair exploring a Greek and a Roman who shared similar qualities or roles. He paired Theseus (founder of Athens as a unified city) with Romulus (founder of Rome) and wrote an explicit comparison of the two. Plutarch noted that both heroes had uncertain births (divine or semi-divine fathers, mothers of uncertain status), both unified scattered communities into a single great city, and both committed acts of violence — Theseus abandoning Ariadne; Romulus killing Remus — that cast a shadow over their achievements. Plutarch’s comparison is a sophisticated literary work that invites readers to think about what kind of character a founder needs and what moral compromises city-building demands. For this exam, the key use of Plutarch is to show that ancient authors themselves compared Athens and Rome through their foundation heroes.

Modern historians do not take the stories of Romulus and Remus or the contest of Athena and Poseidon as literal history. However, there is real archaeological evidence for early settlement at Rome and Athens. The question is not “did it happen?” but “what did the myth mean?” Foundation myths told citizens who they were, who their city belonged to, and what values it stood for. They were performed in drama, displayed in public art, and recited in religious ceremonies. Even Livy, writing a careful history of Rome, included the Romulus and Remus story while acknowledging that such tales “adorn” the origins of cities — he did not expect his readers to believe every detail literally, but he recognised that the stories shaped Roman identity in ways no dry list of facts could replace.

lessons.title: Myth as a Symbol of Power

before.content_html:
Myth as a Political Language

In the ancient world, myth was not merely entertainment. The myths chosen for public display in temples, on friezes, on altars and in statues carried deliberate political messages. When a ruler or a city chose to depict a particular battle between gods and monsters, or a hero defeating savagery, they were making a statement about themselves: we are the forces of order, civilisation and divine favour; our enemies are chaos and barbarism. Understanding how myth was used to express power requires reading ancient art not just aesthetically but politically — asking not only “what does this show?” but “why was this chosen, and what did it communicate to its audience?”

The Centauromachy on the Parthenon

The Parthenon in Athens, completed in 438 BC, was the most spectacular expression of Athenian power and pride. Its sculptures were designed as an integrated programme of mythological messaging. On the metopes — the carved panels between the triglyphs on the exterior of the temple — the south side depicted the Centauromachy: the battle between the Lapiths (a Greek people) and the Centaurs. The story was that the Centaurs had been invited to a wedding feast and, drunk on wine, attacked the Lapith women and attempted to carry them off. In the marble metopes, the conflict is shown in vivid, energetic relief: each panel shows a single combat between a Lapith and a Centaur, muscles straining, limbs entwined, the victory of civilised form over bestial violence. The Centaurs are wild and ungainly; the Lapiths are controlled and graceful even in struggle.

The message was transparent to any educated Greek viewer: the Lapiths represented Athens and the Greeks; the Centaurs represented the Persians, who had invaded Greece in 480–479 BC and been driven back by Athenian courage. This mythological allegory allowed the Athenians to celebrate their military victory in religious, universal terms: we did not merely defeat invaders, we defeated barbarism itself.

Key Fact

The south metopes of the Parthenon show the Centauromachy. Each of the thirty-two panels (originally) showed a single combat between a Lapith and a Centaur. The choice of this myth was deliberate: Centaurs represented barbarism and disorder; Lapiths represented Greek civilisation. The parallel with the Persian Wars was clear to every Athenian who approached the temple.

The Amazonomachy on the Bassae Frieze

The Temple of Apollo at Bassae (in the Peloponnese) had a continuous interior frieze — now in the British Museum — depicting two battles: a Amazonomachy (Greeks fighting the Amazons) and a Centauromachy. The Bassae frieze, carved in the late fifth century BC, is remarkable for its dynamic composition: figures pile on top of one another, weapons clash, Amazons in exotic eastern costumes fight Greek heroes. The Amazon myth was particularly rich in political symbolism. The Amazons were a race of warrior women from the east — their very existence violated Greek social norms (women who fought, who rejected men, who came from the barbaric east). Defeating them in myth meant defeating the “other” in the most complete possible sense: not just a foreign people, but a foreign way of ordering the world.

Both the Centauromachy and the Amazonomachy served the same political-mythological function: they mapped Greek victory over a monstrous or barbaric “other” onto the Greek experience of the Persian Wars. The Centaurs and the Amazons were both perceived as threats to the Greek social order — Centaurs represented uncontrolled animal appetite; Amazons represented a world with the sexes inverted. By showing Greek heroes defeating these mythological enemies, the art celebrated not just military power but the rightness of the Greek way of life. It also worked religiously: these battles took place on sacred buildings dedicated to the gods, implying divine approval of the Greek cause. The gods themselves endorsed the defeat of chaos.

Augustus and the Use of Myth

No ruler of the ancient world used myth more systematically as a tool of political power than Augustus, the first Roman emperor. After the chaos of the civil wars that destroyed the Roman Republic, Augustus presented himself as the restorer of peace and order — and he anchored that claim in myth and religion. He rebuilt temples, revived ancient rituals and embedded himself in Rome’s divine mythology at every opportunity.

The Augustus of Prima Porta statue communicates his power through layered mythological reference. Augustus stands in the pose of a Roman commander, his arm extended as if addressing troops. His breastplate (cuirass) is covered with carved scenes: at the centre, a Parthian commander returning Roman military standards to a Roman general — a real diplomatic triumph of 20 BC that Augustus used as propaganda. Above this scene the sky god (Caelus) holds out his canopy of stars; below sits the earth goddess (Terra), surrounded by symbols of plenty. Sol (the sun) and Aurora (the dawn) drive their chariots at the sides. The whole breastplate presents the Roman world as cosmically ordered under Augustus’s leadership. At the base of the statue, Cupid rides a dolphin — a clear reference to Augustus’s claimed descent through Julius Caesar to Aeneas and then to Venus herself. The statue does not just show a soldier; it shows a man whose rule is woven into the fabric of the universe.

Key Fact

The Augustus of Prima Porta statue (Vatican Museum) is the supreme example of Roman myth used as political propaganda: the breastplate cosmogram, the Cupid dolphin reference to Venus, and the oratorical pose all work together to present Augustus as divinely sanctioned ruler of a cosmically ordered empire.

The Ara Pacis of Augustus

The Ara Pacis (Altar of Augustan Peace), dedicated in 9 BC, was a marble altar enclosed within carved walls. The monument worked on two levels simultaneously. At the literal level, it celebrated a real event: Augustus’s return from successful campaigns in Spain and Gaul in 13 BC, and the peace he brought. At the mythological level, its relief panels embedded this peace in a divine narrative. One panel showed Aeneas making a sacrifice — the ancestor of Rome, the Trojan hero, performing the same pious act of thanksgiving that Augustus was now repeating, showing Roman history as one long sacred covenant between the people and the gods. Another panel showed the goddess Roma seated in armour on a throne of captured weapons, serene and powerful. A third showed a mother goddess (possibly Pax, goddess of peace, or Venus) seated with abundant natural gifts around her — children, animals, flowing water and grain. The overall message: peace, fertility, divine blessing and cosmic order had all arrived with Augustus.

Both Greek and Roman uses of myth for political purposes share the same basic logic: myth gives events a cosmic, divine frame that makes them seem inevitable and approved by the gods. But there are important differences. Greek mythological allegory (the Parthenon Centauromachy; the Bassae Amazonomachy) tended to be indirect — it did not show Athenians fighting Persians directly but encoded the message in mythological form. Roman uses of myth under Augustus were often more direct and personal: the Augustus of Prima Porta puts the emperor himself at the centre of the mythological cosmos; the Ara Pacis shows his family in procession alongside mythological allegories. The Roman emperor was the link between the divine world and the human world in a way no Athenian democratic politician could ever be.

The World of the Dead

In ancient Greek and Roman belief, death was not the end but a journey to a different realm. The dead passed into the Underworld, an underground kingdom whose geography was carefully mapped in myth and literature. Two rivers defined the boundary between life and death: the Styx was the great oath-river of the gods, whose waters were used for the most binding divine promises. The Acheron (river of woe) was the river across which the dead were ferried. Other rivers included Lethe (forgetfulness) and Phlegethon (fire).

Charon, the ferryman, waited at the riverbank to carry newly dead souls across. He required payment: a coin called an obol was placed on the tongue or over the eyes of the corpse at burial to ensure the dead could pay their fare. Those without payment were left to wander on the near bank for a hundred years before Charon would take them across for free. This belief directly shaped burial practice — to be buried without a coin was to be abandoned between the worlds, unable to rest.

Key Fact

The Greek Underworld was ruled by Hades and his queen Persephone. Its entrance was guarded by Cerberus, a monstrous three-headed dog. The souls of the dead were judged by three judges (Minos, Rhadamanthus and Aeacus) and sent to different regions: Elysium for the virtuous and heroic, the Asphodel Meadows for ordinary souls, and Tartarus for the wicked, where they suffered eternal punishment.

The Abduction of Persephone: The Homeric Hymn to Demeter

One of the most important mythological accounts of the Underworld is told in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter. The hymn opens with the young goddess Persephone picking flowers in a meadow when the earth suddenly opens and Hades seizes her, dragging her down into his kingdom to be his bride. Her mother Demeter, goddess of the harvest, hears her daughter’s cry and begins a frantic search across the earth. In her grief, Demeter abandons her role as harvest goddess: the crops fail, the earth becomes barren and humans begin to starve.

Zeus eventually intervenes, sending Hermes to retrieve Persephone from the Underworld. But before she leaves, Hades gives her pomegranate seeds to eat. In the rules of the Underworld, anyone who eats food in Hades’ realm is bound to return. Because she had eaten, Persephone could not remain entirely in the upper world: a compromise was reached. She would spend part of each year with her mother on earth (spring and summer — when Demeter rejoices and the earth blooms) and part of each year with Hades below (autumn and winter — when Demeter grieves and the crops die). The hymn is thus a myth of origins: it explains the cycle of the seasons through a story of divine grief, loss and partial recovery.

The Homeric Hymn to Demeter is not merely a story about seasons: it is closely connected to the Eleusinian Mysteries, a secret religious cult held at Eleusis (near Athens) in which initiates underwent rituals connected to Demeter and Persephone. The Mysteries promised initiates a blessed afterlife — a better fate in the Underworld than ordinary souls received. The hymn ends with Demeter establishing a sacred rite at Eleusis and declaring that those who are initiated will be blessed in this life and honoured in death. The hymn is therefore both a mythological narrative about the seasons and a sacred text explaining why the Mysteries existed and what they offered. This is a classic example of myth and religion working together: the story (Persephone’s return) underpins and explains the ritual (initiation at Eleusis).

Orpheus and Eurydice: Ovid’s Metamorphoses

The Roman poet Ovid retold the story of Orpheus in his Metamorphoses (10.1–64). Orpheus was a musician of such extraordinary skill that his playing could charm animals, move stones and bend the laws of the natural world. When his wife Eurydice died on their wedding day — bitten by a snake while walking through the grass with her naiad companions — Orpheus could not accept her death. He descended into the Underworld — a feat that the living were not supposed to be able to achieve — and played his lyre before Hades and Persephone. The music was so beautiful and so full of grief that it moved the king and queen of the dead to tears. Even the punishments of the wicked in Tartarus paused: Sisyphus sat on his boulder, the wheel of Ixion stopped turning. Hades agreed to release Eurydice on one condition: Orpheus must lead her back to the upper world without looking back.

Orpheus led Eurydice upward through the dark passages of the Underworld. As they approached the exit and the light of the upper world was almost upon them, he could no longer resist the overwhelming urge to see whether she was truly following. He turned back to look. At that moment Eurydice slipped back into death, reaching her arms towards him as she was pulled away. Orpheus had failed by a single glance. Ovid’s version is intensely psychological: it is not cowardice or disbelief that destroys Orpheus, but love itself, which cannot accept the rules of the world it operates in.

Key Fact

Ovid’s account of Orpheus and Eurydice in Metamorphoses 10.1–64 is a prescribed literary source. Key details to know: in Ovid's Metamorphoses 10, Eurydice died from a snake bite while walking through the grass with her naiad companions on her wedding day; Orpheus descended to Hades and moved the underworld rulers with his music; he was given the condition of not looking back; he failed and lost Eurydice a second time. After this, Orpheus refused all further human love and was eventually killed by the Maenads (followers of Dionysos).

Heracles and Cerberus

The twelfth and final labour of Heracles required him to descend into the Underworld and bring back Cerberus, the three-headed guardian hound. This labour was the most extraordinary because it demanded something no mortal was supposed to do: enter Hades’ kingdom while still alive and leave again. Heracles achieved it through a combination of force and divine assistance. According to various ancient accounts, he first sought initiation into the Eleusinian Mysteries to prepare himself (connecting the Heracles myth to the Demeter cult). He then descended, disarmed Cerberus and dragged him to the surface. The dog was shown to King Eurystheus (who, predictably, fled in terror) and then returned to the Underworld. This labour represented the ultimate conquest: not of a monster in the world above, but of death itself. It was the act that most clearly pointed towards Heracles’ eventual apotheosis — the man who could conquer Hades was not far from becoming a god.

Greek and Roman accounts of the Underworld are broadly similar — both involve rivers, a ferryman, a guardian creature, a king and queen, and regions for different kinds of dead — because the Romans largely adopted the Greek mythological tradition. But there are differences in emphasis. In Ovid’s telling of Orpheus and Eurydice, the Underworld is shown as strangely responsive to emotion: Hades and Persephone weep, the punishments pause. This is a characteristically Roman, humanised portrayal. Virgil’s Aeneid Book 6 (not a prescribed text but useful contextual knowledge) gives the most systematic Latin account of the Underworld: Aeneas descends to speak with his dead father and is shown the whole realm, including the souls of Romans yet to be born. This gives the Underworld a specifically Roman purpose — it is the repository of Rome’s future greatness. The Greek Underworld, as portrayed in the Hymn to Demeter, is a darker, more terrifying place of permanent loss.

knowledge_checks.q: In the Homeric Hymn to Demeter, why could Persephone not return permanently to the upper world?
options: Hades refused to let her go
She had eaten pomegranate seeds in the Underworld

knowledge_checks.q: In Ovid's Metamorphoses, what single condition did Hades give Orpheus when releasing Eurydice?
options: He must leave his lyre behind
He must not speak until they reached the upper world
He must not look back at Eurydice on the way out
He must bring a living animal as payment

practice_questions.text: Name the ferryman of the Greek Underworld who carried the souls of the dead across the river.
Describe the character of Hades' kingdom as presented in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three accurate details from or connected to the Hymn: it is a dark realm beneath the earth; it is the realm of permanent death and loss; Persephone is seized and taken there against her will; it is governed by rules (eating food in Hades binds one to return); even the gods must negotiate with Hades (Zeus sends Hermes as a mediator); the pomegranate episode shows the Underworld has binding legal power; it is a place of grief for those left behind (Demeter’s famine).

practice_questions.text:
Read the following summary of an episode from a Roman poet's account of a visit to the Underworld:

A young man, his lyre in hand, descended through the darkness to plead for his dead wife. When he played before the king and queen of the dead, even the most hardened inhabitants of that grim place felt his grief. The tortured souls paused their sufferings to listen; the judges of the dead were moved. The king agreed to release the young man's wife on a single condition, which would prove impossible to keep.

Using the passage and your own knowledge, explain what this episode tells us about Roman ideas of the Underworld and the power of love.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5): Analyses at least three specific elements of the source with precise own-knowledge support. Identifies this as Ovid’s Metamorphoses 10.1–64; the hero is Orpheus and his wife is Eurydice. ‘Even the tortured souls paused’ = the Underworld in Ovid is responsive to human emotion in a way that Greek sources often don’t show; ‘the judges of the dead were moved’ = the power of art and love temporarily overcomes divine law; the ‘condition impossible to keep’ = Orpheus’s fatal glance back; the Underworld’s rules are absolute even when bent by beauty. Evaluates what this reveals about Ovid’s Roman portrayal of the Underworld as humanised and emotionally rich, contrasting with the darker Greek version in the Hymn to Demeter.
Secure (4): Analyses two elements; names Ovid and Orpheus; some comment on what the episode reveals.
Developing (3): Identifies one or two details; largely descriptive.
Emerging (1–2): Retells the story with little analysis.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the Homeric Hymn to Demeter links the story of Persephone to the natural world.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for explaining Demeter’s role (goddess of the harvest, responsible for crops and fertility); 1 mark for explaining what happened when she stopped (she abandoned her divine role, causing famine and drought); 1 mark for the pomegranate compromise (Persephone must spend part of the year below = winter; part above = spring/summer); 1 mark for the wider significance (the myth ‘explains’ the cycle of the seasons through a divine story of loss and partial recovery; it shows Greek religious thought connecting natural phenomena to divine action).

practice_questions.text: How similar are the Greek and Roman accounts of the Underworld and journeys to it? Use named sources to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Sustained argument comparing both cultures. Similarities: both share the same geography (rivers, ferryman Charon, three-headed guardian Cerberus, ruler Hades/Pluto and Persephone, regions for different souls); both involve journeys by exceptional figures (Heracles, Orpheus/Persephone); both use the Underworld as a frame for exploring death, loss and the possibility of return. Differences: the Hymn to Demeter presents a harsh, legally rigid Underworld where even Zeus must compromise; Ovid’s Underworld is emotionally responsive (Hades and Persephone weep; punishments pause); the Roman version tends to humanise the Underworld more. Heracles in both cultures = mortal mastery over death = apotheosis. Uses named sources (Homeric Hymn to Demeter 1–104, 301–474; Ovid Metamorphoses 10.1–64). Reaches a supported conclusion.
Secure (5–6): Covers both similarities and differences; names both sources; clear argument.
Developing (3–4): Some relevant comparisons; limited source use.
Emerging (1–2): Describes one myth without comparing.

practice_questions.text: Give two rules or conditions that governed the Underworld in ancient Greek and Roman myth.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two of: the dead must pay Charon to cross (coin placed in the mouth or on the eyes); anyone who eats food in the Underworld is bound to return (pomegranate rule; Persephone); a living person who enters must not look back when leaving (Orpheus); those not properly buried must wait 100 years before Charon takes them; Cerberus prevents the living from entering and the dead from leaving.

before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Greek Underworld was a carefully structured realm ruled by Hades and Persephone, entered across the river Acheron by paying Charon the ferryman; its gate was guarded by the three-headed Cerberus.
  • The prescribed Homeric Hymn to Demeter (lines 1–104, 301–474) uses Persephone’s abduction and partial return to explain the seasons and to underpin the Eleusinian Mysteries, linking myth directly to religious ritual.
  • Ovid’s Metamorphoses 10.1–64 tells the story of Orpheus and Eurydice: Orpheus’s music moved the Underworld rulers to tears, but his failure to obey the single condition (not looking back) shows the absolute power of the Underworld’s laws even over love.

glossary_terms.definition: The realm of the dead in ancient Greek and Roman belief, ruled by Hades (Greek) or Pluto (Roman); a vast underground kingdom divided into regions for the different kinds of dead.

The river of hatred in the Greek Underworld and the oath-river of the gods; the Olympians swore their most solemn and binding oaths by it. The dead were ferried across the Acheron (not the Styx) by Charon.
The ferryman of the Underworld who carried the souls of the dead across the river Acheron in return for an obol (coin); the dead were buried with a coin placed on their tongue or eyes to pay him.
The three-headed dog that guarded the entrance to the Underworld, preventing the living from entering and the dead from leaving.
A long Homeric Hymn telling the story of Persephone's abduction by Hades and Demeter's grief and search; it explains the origin of the seasons and the Eleusinian Mysteries.
The legendary musician and poet of Greek and Roman myth who descended into the Underworld to retrieve his dead wife Eurydice; his story is told by Ovid in Metamorphoses 10.1–64.
